flavor-rotation-7e227c98.title: Flavor Rotation

V_{CKM}.name: CKM Matrix
V_{CKM}.description: The 3x3 Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa unitary matrix that describes the weak flavor mixing of quarks.

V_{ud}.name: CKM Matrix Element (up-down)
V_{ud}.description: The amplitude for a down quark to transform into an up quark via the weak interaction.

V_{us}.name: CKM Matrix Element (up-strange)
V_{us}.description: The amplitude for a strange quark to transform into an up quark via the weak interaction, or a down quark to transform into a strange quark.

V_{ub}.name: CKM Matrix Element (up-bottom)
V_{ub}.description: The amplitude for a bottom quark to transform into an up quark via the weak interaction, or a down quark to transform into a bottom quark.

V_{cd}.name: CKM Matrix Element (charm-down)
V_{cd}.description: The amplitude for a charm quark to transform into a down quark via the weak interaction, or a strange quark to transform into a down quark.

V_{cs}.name: CKM Matrix Element (charm-strange)
V_{cs}.description: The amplitude for a strange quark to transform into a charm quark via the weak interaction, or a charm quark to transform into a strange quark.

V_{cb}.name: CKM Matrix Element (charm-bottom)
V_{cb}.description: The amplitude for a bottom quark to transform into a charm quark via the weak interaction, or a charm quark to transform into a bottom quark.

V_{td}.name: CKM Matrix Element (top-down)
V_{td}.description: The amplitude for a top quark to transform into a down quark via the weak interaction, or a bottom quark to transform into a down quark.

V_{ts}.name: CKM Matrix Element (top-strange)
V_{ts}.description: The amplitude for a top quark to transform into a strange quark via the weak interaction, or a bottom quark to transform into a strange quark.

V_{tb}.name: CKM Matrix Element (top-bottom)
V_{tb}.description: The amplitude for a bottom quark to transform into a top quark via the weak interaction, or a top quark to transform into a bottom quark.

\\(V\\).name: Electric Potential
\\(V\\).description: The amount of work energy needed to move a unit of electric charge from a reference point to a specific point in an electric field.

flavor-rotation-7e227c98.interpretation: The CKM matrix is a fundamental component of the Standard Model, encoding information about quark mixing in weak interactions. Each element $V_{ij}$ of the matrix represents the probability amplitude for a quark of flavor $i$ in one generation to transform into a quark of flavor $j$ in another generation through the weak force. For example, $V_{ud}$ is the amplitude for a down quark to transform into an up quark, $V_{us}$ for a down quark to transform into a strange quark, and $V_{ub}$ for a down quark to transform into a bottom quark. Similarly, the second row relates to the strange quark, and the third row to the bottom quark. The unitarity of the matrix ($V V^\dagger = V^\dagger V = I$) ensures that probabilities are conserved. The complex entries in the matrix (beyond the three real parameters that can be fixed by rephasing quark fields) are the source of CP violation in the quark sector, a crucial phenomenon for explaining the matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe.
flavor-rotation-7e227c98.symmetry_origin: The CKM matrix arises from the fact that the mass terms for quarks in the Standard Model Lagrangian are not diagonal in the flavor basis. After diagonalizing the quark mass matrices separately for quarks of different weak isospin ($I_3 = +1/2$ and $I_3 = -1/2$), a unitary transformation is required to relate the mass eigenstates to the flavor (interaction) eigenstates. This transformation is represented by the CKM matrix. The existence of three generations of quarks necessitates a $3 \times 3$ matrix. The freedom to choose the phase of each quark mass eigenstate allows for the parameterization of the CKM matrix in terms of three real parameters (two angles and one complex phase) and a potential overall phase that can be absorbed.
flavor-rotation-7e227c98.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where there is only one generation of quarks, the CKM matrix would be a $1 \times 1$ identity matrix, implying no flavor mixing. In scenarios with two generations (e.g., neglecting the top quark), the CKM matrix is a $2 \times 2$ unitary matrix, parameterized by a single angle (the Cabibbo angle), representing mixing only between the first and second generations. The presence of the third generation and the CKM matrix's complex phase allow for CP violation. Extreme values of the matrix elements would imply very strong or very weak mixing between specific quark flavors.
flavor-rotation-7e227c98.conceptual_definition: The Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix, denoted as $V_{CKM}$, is a $3 \times 3$ unitary matrix that describes the mixing of quarks in the weak interaction. In the Standard Model of particle physics, weak interactions do not diagonalize the mass matrices for quarks. The CKM matrix quantifies the transformation between the quark mass eigenstates and the quark flavor eigenstates, which are the states that participate in the weak force. Specifically, it describes the probabilities of flavor-changing weak decays, such as a down quark decaying into an up quark, or a strange quark decaying into a down quark.
flavor-rotation-7e227c98.intuitive_summary: The CKM matrix quantifies how much each type of quark 'mixes' with other types during weak interactions, governing the probabilities of flavor-changing decays.

structural-type-3a28090c.title: Structural Type (Polytropic Relations)

\u0301gamma.name: Structural Type (Polytropic Relations)
\u0301gamma.description: A dimensionless index that characterizes the structural type or scaling properties of a system described by a polytropic relation. It is derived from the parameter 'n'.

n.name: Polytropic Parameter
n.description: A dimensionless parameter that defines the specific form of the polytropic relation, typically as P ∝ ́rho^n. This parameter dictates the physical behavior of the system.

\\(\\gamma\\).name: Lorentz Factor
\\(\\gamma\\).description: The relativistic scale factor describing time dilation and length contraction.

structural-type-3a28090c.interpretation: In this equation, ́gamma represents a structural type index related to the polytropic process being described. The variable 'n' is a parameter that defines the specific form of the polytropic relation. Specifically, if a polytropic process is defined by the relation P = Ḱrho^́nu, then ́gamma is related to ́nu. In many contexts, ́nu itself is identified with 'n', leading to the direct relation ́gamma = 1 + 1/n. This formula quantifies how the nature of the relationship between pressure and density (defined by 'n') dictates the overall structural behavior or scaling properties of the system.
structural-type-3a28090c.symmetry_origin: The origin of this relationship lies in the mathematical framework used to describe self-similar solutions to differential equations governing physical systems, particularly in areas like hydrostatics and thermodynamics. When seeking solutions of the form ́rho(r) − ́rho_c (r/R_c)^́nu, where ́rho is density, ́rho_c is central density, r is radius, R_c is a characteristic radius, and ́nu is the polytropic exponent, the resulting Lane-Emden equation can be solved using a parameter 'n' which dictates the specific polytropic relation. The ́gamma parameter then characterizes the resulting structure's scaling properties.
structural-type-3a28090c.limits_and_boundary: As 'n' approaches infinity (́n → ∞), ́gamma approaches 1 (́gamma → 1). This corresponds to an isothermal sphere, where the temperature is constant, and the pressure is directly proportional to the density (P ∝ ́rho). As 'n' approaches 1 (́n → 1), ́gamma approaches 2 (́gamma → 2). This corresponds to a polytrope of index 1, which has specific mathematical properties related to pressure being proportional to density squared (P ∝ ́rho^2). Special cases arise for specific integer values of 'n' (e.g., n=3 for a fully convective star).
structural-type-3a28090c.conceptual_definition: This formula defines the relationship between the polytropic index, often denoted as ́gamma, and the parameter 'n' which characterizes the specific form of a polytropic relation. Polytropic relations are used to describe thermodynamically self-similar processes, commonly found in astrophysics (e.g., stellar structure, gas spheres) and fluid dynamics, where the pressure is related to density by a power law: P = K ́rho^́nu, where P is pressure, ́rho is density, K is a constant, and ́nu is the polytropic exponent. The ́gamma in this formula is not the adiabatic index but a related structural index.
structural-type-3a28090c.intuitive_summary: The structural type of a polytropic relation, represented by ́gamma, is directly determined by the power-law exponent 'n' in its definition.

light-freedom-307c4a16.title: Light Freedom

z_{rec}.name: Redshift at Recombination
z_{rec}.description: The redshift parameter corresponding to the epoch of recombination, when the universe transitioned from an opaque plasma to a transparent, neutral gas. A value of approximately 1,100 indicates that the universe has expanded by a factor of about 1,101 since that time.

\\(z\\).name: Position Coordinate
\\(z\\).description: A coordinate representing the longitudinal or altitude location of a particle in space.

light-freedom-307c4a16.interpretation: In this formula, \(z_{rec}\) represents the redshift at the time of recombination. Redshift is a measure of how much the universe has expanded since a particular event occurred. A redshift of \(z\) means that the wavelength of light has been stretched by a factor of \(1+z\). The value \(z_{rec} \approx 1,100\) signifies that the universe has expanded by a factor of approximately \(1+1100 = 1101\) since the epoch of recombination. This specific redshift is significant because it corresponds to the moment when the universe cooled enough (around 3,000 Kelvin) for electrons and protons to combine and form neutral hydrogen atoms. Before recombination, the universe was an ionized plasma, opaque to photons. After recombination, photons could travel freely, leading to the formation of the Cosmic Microwave Background radiation we observe today, redshifted from its original frequency. The number \(1,100\) is derived from detailed cosmological models that consider the density of matter and radiation in the early universe, the physics of atomic hydrogen, and the expansion rate.
light-freedom-307c4a16.symmetry_origin: The value of \(z_{rec}\) is not directly derived from a fundamental symmetry principle in the same way that conservation laws arise from spacetime symmetries (e.g., Noether's theorem). Instead, it is a consequence of the thermodynamic and cosmological evolution of the universe, governed by the Friedmann equations and the physics of matter-energy content. The calculation involves the Saha ionization equation, which describes the degree of ionization of a gas as a function of temperature and pressure, and the expansion rate of the universe. Therefore, its origin lies in the interplay of general relativity describing cosmic expansion and statistical mechanics/quantum mechanics describing atomic processes.
light-freedom-307c4a16.limits_and_boundary: As the universe expands indefinitely (approaching infinite future time), the redshift of any light source would approach -1, meaning wavelengths would be infinitely stretched towards infinite values, though this is a theoretical limit. In the context of recombination, the formula gives a specific, non-extreme value. If we were to consider an ever-contracting universe approaching the Big Bang singularity, the redshift would theoretically approach infinity, implying an extremely hot and dense early state. However, the formula specifically quantifies the redshift at the transition point of recombination, which is a particular historical epoch, not an asymptotic limit of the universe's expansion history.
light-freedom-307c4a16.conceptual_definition: The formula provides an approximate value for the redshift at recombination, denoted as \(z_{rec}\). This redshift marks a critical epoch in the early universe when it cooled sufficiently for neutral atoms to form, allowing photons to decouple from matter and travel freely. This event is directly observable through the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) radiation. The value \(1,100\) is a widely accepted approximation for this redshift.
light-freedom-307c4a16.intuitive_summary: The universe's transition from an opaque plasma to a transparent neutral gas occurred when its scale factor had expanded by a factor of approximately 1,100, causing the light to 'decouple'.

horizon-shape-bcfacb0e.title: Horizon Shape

ds^2.name: Spacetime Interval
ds^2.description: The infinitesimal spacetime interval, representing the 'distance' between two infinitesimally close events in spacetime. It is a fundamental quantity in relativity that is invariant under coordinate transformations.

f(r).name: Metric Function
f(r).description: A function of the radial coordinate that determines the geometry of spacetime. In the Schwarzschild metric, it governs the time dilation and radial stretching due to gravity.

d\\tau.name: Proper Time
d\\tau.description: The infinitesimal interval of proper time, which is the time measured by an observer's clock moving along a worldline through spacetime.

dr.name: Proper Radial Distance
dr.description: The infinitesimal interval of proper radial distance, representing the physical distance measured radially outward from the central mass.

r.name: Radial Coordinate
r.description: The radial coordinate in spherical symmetry. It is often defined such that the surface area of a sphere is 4πr^2, analogous to Euclidean geometry.

d\\Omega^2.name: Solid Angle Element
d\\Omega^2.description: The infinitesimal element of solid angle, which describes the angular part of the spacetime interval. For spherical symmetry, it is given by d\Omega^2 = d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta d\phi^2, where \(\theta\) is the polar angle and \(\phi\) is the azimuthal angle.

G.name: Gravitational Constant
G.description: The fundamental constant of proportionality in Newton's law of universal gravitation and Einstein's field equations, quantifying the strength of gravitational interaction.

M.name: Mass
M.description: The mass of the central, non-rotating, spherically symmetric object creating the gravitational field.

c.name: Speed of Light
c.description: The speed of light in a vacuum, a universal physical constant representing the maximum speed at which energy, matter, and information can travel.

\\(d\\).name: Total Differential
\\(d\\).description: Represents an infinitesimal change in a variable (e.g. dx, dt).

\\(s\\).name: Seconds / Proper Time Interval
\\(s\\).description: The SI unit of time, or the invariant interval traversed by a clock.

\\(f\\).name: Frequency
\\(f\\).description: The number of occurrences of a repeating event per unit of time.

\\(\\tau\\).name: Infinitesimal Volume Element
\\(\\tau\\).description: An infinitesimal region of space over which a volume integration is performed.

\\(\\Omega\\).name: Solid Angle / Resistance / Omega Baryon
\\(\\Omega\\).description: 3D spatial projection angle, electrical impedance unit, or strangeness -3 hyperon.

horizon-shape-bcfacb0e.interpretation:
The equation 
$$ds^2 = f(r) d\tau^2 + f(r)^{-1} dr^2 + r^2 d\Omega^2$$ 
represents the infinitesimal spacetime interval, \(ds^2\), in a coordinate system around a spherical mass. 
\(d\tau^2\) is the infinitesimal proper time interval, which is the time measured by a clock moving along the worldline. The term 
$$f(r) d\tau^2$$ 
shows how the proper time is dilated due to the gravitational potential. 
\(dr^2\) is the infinitesimal proper radial distance squared. The factor 
$$f(r)^{-1}$$ 
illustrates how radial distances are stretched by gravity. 
\(r^2 d\Omega^2\) represents the infinitesimal proper area element on a sphere of radius 
\(r\) (where 
\(d\Omega^2 = d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta d\phi^2\) is the solid angle element), which is unchanged from Euclidean geometry due to the spherical symmetry. The function 
\(f(r)\) is typically given by 
$$f(r) = 1 - \frac{2GM}{c^2r}$$ 
in the Schwarzschild solution, where 
\(G\) is the gravitational constant, 
\(M\) is the mass of the central object, and 
\(c\) is the speed of light. The term 
$$\frac{2GM}{c^2}$$ 
is the Schwarzschild radius, often denoted 
\(r_s\).
horizon-shape-bcfacb0e.symmetry_origin: This metric is derived from Einstein's field equations of general relativity, specifically for the case of a static, spherically symmetric vacuum spacetime. The spherical symmetry implies that the spacetime geometry is the same in all directions from the central mass and does not change with time. This symmetry simplifies the field equations considerably, leading to this particular solution.
horizon-shape-bcfacb0e.limits_and_boundary:
As the radial coordinate 
\(r\) approaches infinity (
\(r \to \infty\)), the function 
\(f(r) \to 1\). In this limit, the metric becomes 
$$ds^2 \approx d\tau^2 + dr^2 + r^2 d\Omega^2$$ 
which is the Minkowski metric of flat spacetime, indicating that far from the mass, spacetime behaves as if there were no gravity. As 
\(r\) approaches the Schwarzschild radius 
\(r_s = \frac{2GM}{c^2}\), the term 
\(f(r)\) approaches zero (
\(f(r) \to 0\)). This causes the coefficient of 
\(dr^2\) to diverge, while the coefficient of 
\(d\tau^2\) goes to zero. This divergence signifies the event horizon, where spacetime is so warped that light cannot escape, and time and radial space coordinates effectively swap roles in terms of their behavior.
horizon-shape-bcfacb0e.conceptual_definition: The formula provided, known as the Schwarzschild metric (or a generalized version thereof), describes the spacetime geometry around a non-rotating, spherically symmetric mass. It is a solution to Einstein's field equations in general relativity and dictates how distances and time intervals are measured in the vicinity of such a mass, particularly near the event horizon of a black hole.
horizon-shape-bcfacb0e.intuitive_summary: This equation quantifies how the curvature of spacetime, caused by a mass, warps both radial and angular measurements, and affects the flow of time.

spatial-energy-8be8ff08.title: Spatial Energy

U_{field}.name: Spatial Energy
U_{field}.description: The total potential energy stored in the electromagnetic field within a given volume.

\\varepsilon_0.name: Permittivity of free space
\\varepsilon_0.description: A fundamental physical constant representing the capability of a vacuum to permit electric fields.

E.name: Electric field magnitude
E.description: The magnitude of the electric field vector at a point in space.

\\mu_0.name: Permeability of free space
\\mu_0.description: A fundamental physical constant representing the ability of a vacuum to support the formation of a magnetic field.

B.name: Magnetic field magnitude
B.description: The magnitude of the magnetic field vector at a point in space.

d\\tau.name: Volume element
d\\tau.description: An infinitesimal element of volume over which the integration is performed.

\\(\\epsilon_0\\).name: Vacuum Permittivity
\\(\\epsilon_0\\).description: The capability of the vacuum to permit electric field lines.

\\(U\\).name: Potential Energy
\\(U\\).description: Position-dependent stored energy of a system.

\\(d\\).name: Total Differential
\\(d\\).description: Represents an infinitesimal change in a variable (e.g. dx, dt).

\\(\\tau\\).name: Infinitesimal Volume Element
\\(\\tau\\).description: An infinitesimal region of space over which a volume integration is performed.

spatial-energy-8be8ff08.interpretation:
This equation describes the energy stored in electromagnetic fields. The term 
$$\varepsilon_0 E^2$$
 represents the energy density of the electric field, where 
$$\varepsilon_0$$
 is the permittivity of free space and 
$$\(E\)$$
 is the magnitude of the electric field vector. The term 
$$\frac{1}{\mu_0} B^2$$
 represents the energy density of the magnetic field, where 
$$\mu_0$$
 is the permeability of free space and 
$$\(B\)$$
 is the magnitude of the magnetic field vector. The factor of 
$$\frac{1}{2}$$
 arises from the way electric and magnetic fields are generated and interact. The integral 
$$\int d\tau$$
 indicates that this energy density is summed over an entire volume 
$$\tau$$
 in space to obtain the total stored energy 
$$\(U_{field}\) $$.
spatial-energy-8be8ff08.symmetry_origin: This formula is derived from Maxwell's equations and is a fundamental consequence of the wave nature of electromagnetic radiation and the conservation of energy in electromagnetism. It is invariant under Lorentz transformations, reflecting the relativistic nature of electromagnetism.
spatial-energy-8be8ff08.limits_and_boundary:
In regions where the electric field 
$$\(E\)$$
 and magnetic field 
$$\(B\)$$
 are zero, the energy density is also zero. As the fields approach infinity (e.g., in the presence of charged particles or currents), the stored energy density also tends towards infinity, subject to the integration volume. In the absence of time-varying fields, this represents static field energy.
spatial-energy-8be8ff08.conceptual_definition:
The formula 
$$U_{field} = \frac{1}{2} \int (\varepsilon_0 E^2 + \frac{1}{\mu_0} B^2) d\tau$$ 
represents the total potential energy stored in electromagnetic fields within a given volume of space. It quantifies the energy density associated with electric and magnetic fields, integrated over all space.
spatial-energy-8be8ff08.intuitive_summary: This equation states that energy is stored in electric and magnetic fields, proportional to the square of their strengths.

active-boundary-edde9937.title: Active Boundary

v_F.name: Fermi Velocity
v_F.description: The maximum velocity of particles (fermions) in a system at absolute zero temperature. It represents the velocity of particles at the Fermi surface in momentum space.

\\hbar.name: Reduced Planck Constant
\\hbar.description: A fundamental physical constant that relates the energy of a particle to its frequency and momentum to its wavevector. It is equal to Planck's constant \(h\) divided by \(2\pi\).

k_F.name: Fermi Wavevector
k_F.description: The magnitude of the wavevector corresponding to the Fermi energy. It represents the boundary in momentum space separating occupied and unoccupied states for fermions at absolute zero temperature.

m.name: Particle Mass
m.description: The mass of the individual particles (e.g., electrons) in the system.

\\(v\\).name: Speed / Velocity Magnitude
\\(v\\).description: The rate of change of position with respect to time, representing the speed of a particle.

\\(F\\).name: Force Magnitude
\\(F\\).description: The magnitude of an interaction that causes an object with mass to accelerate.

\\(k\\).name: Spring Stiffness (Hooke's Constant)
\\(k\\).description: The rigidity of a spring or elastic medium, defining restoring force per unit of displacement: $F = -kx$.

active-boundary-edde9937.interpretation: The equation states that the Fermi velocity (\[v_F\]) is directly proportional to the Fermi wavevector (\[k_F\]) and inversely proportional to the mass of the particle (\[m\]), with the reduced Planck constant (\[\hbar\]) serving as the constant of proportionality. The Fermi wavevector (\[k_F\]) represents the maximum momentum a particle can have in a system of non-interacting fermions at absolute zero temperature, corresponding to the boundary of occupied states in momentum space. A larger Fermi wavevector implies particles with higher momentum, and thus higher velocity, assuming constant mass. Conversely, a more massive particle (\[m\]) will have a lower velocity for a given Fermi wavevector, as more energy is required to reach that momentum.
active-boundary-edde9937.symmetry_origin: This formula originates from the quantum mechanical description of a system of non-interacting fermions. In such systems, particles obey the Pauli exclusion principle, meaning no two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state. At absolute zero temperature (\[T=0\text{ K}\)), the fermions fill up all available energy states starting from the lowest energy, up to a maximum energy level called the Fermi energy (\[E_F\)). The boundary of these occupied states in momentum space is defined by the Fermi wavevector (\[k_F\)). The Fermi velocity is then the velocity associated with a particle at this Fermi surface, derived from the non-relativistic energy-momentum relation: \(E = p^2 / (2m)\), where \(p = \hbar k\). Thus, \(E_F = \hbar^2 k_F^2 / (2m)\), and the velocity is \(v_F = dE/dp|_{p=p_F} = p_F/m = \hbar k_F / m\).
active-boundary-edde9937.limits_and_boundary: As the Fermi wavevector (\[k_F\]) approaches zero, the Fermi velocity (\[v_F\]) also approaches zero, indicating a system with very few particles or a very low density where particles occupy only the lowest momentum states. As the mass (\[m\]) of the particles approaches infinity (which is not physically realistic for fundamental particles but can be a conceptual limit), the Fermi velocity also approaches zero, as massive particles are harder to accelerate to high momenta. In practical scenarios within solid-state physics, \(k_F\) is determined by the electron density of the material, and \(m\) is typically the free electron mass.
active-boundary-edde9937.conceptual_definition: The formula describes the Fermi velocity (\(v_F\)), which is the maximum velocity attained by particles in a system at absolute zero temperature. It is particularly relevant in the context of quantum mechanics and solid-state physics, especially for fermions like electrons in a metal. The Fermi velocity is determined by the Fermi wavevector (\(k_F\)) and the mass of the particle (\(m\)), and it is related to fundamental constants like Planck's constant (\[\hbar\]).
active-boundary-edde9937.intuitive_summary: The maximum speed of particles in a quantum system at zero temperature is directly proportional to the momentum scale of that system and inversely proportional to the particle's mass.

local-pdes-29dd35b3.title: Local PDEs

\\(\\mathcal{L}\\).name: Lagrangian Density
\\(\\mathcal{L}\\).description: A function of the field \(\phi\) and its spacetime derivatives \(\partial_\mu \phi\) that defines the dynamics of the field. It is typically expressed in units of energy density.

\\(\\phi\\).name: Field
\\(\\phi\\).unit: dimensionless or specific units depending on field type
\\(\\phi\\).description: The fundamental quantity whose evolution is described by the equation. It can be a scalar, vector, or tensor field, and its units depend on the specific physical system.

\\(\\partial_\\mu\\).name: Spacetime Partial Derivative
\\(\\partial_\\mu\\).description: The partial derivative operator with respect to the \(\mu\)-th spacetime coordinate \(x^\mu\). For a four-vector index \(\mu = 0, 1, 2, 3\), this represents derivatives with respect to time and spatial coordinates.

\\(\\partial_\u03bc \u03c6\\).name: Field Gradient
\\(\\partial_\u03bc \u03c6\\).unit: m^{-1} or specific units depending on field type
\\(\\partial_\u03bc \u03c6\\).description: The spacetime derivative of the field \(\phi\). It represents how the field changes across spacetime.

\\(\\frac{\\partial \\mathcal{L}}{\\part.name: Conjugate Momentum Density
\\(\\frac{\\partial \\mathcal{L}}{\\part.description: The quantity representing the 'momentum' associated with the field \(\phi\) in the direction of the \(\mu\)-th spacetime coordinate. Its units are typically energy density times length, or momentum density.

\\(\\mu\\).name: Reduced Mass / Permeability / Friction Coefficient
\\(\\mu\\).description: Effective inertial mass in two-body problems, magnetic field capability, or surface grip factor.

\\(L\\).name: Angular Momentum Magnitude
\\(L\\).description: The rotational analog of linear momentum.

local-pdes-29dd35b3.interpretation: In this equation, \(\phi\) represents a generalized field, which could be a scalar, vector, or tensor field, and is a function of spacetime coordinates, often denoted as \(x^\mu\) where \(\mu = 0, 1, 2, 3\) in four-dimensional spacetime (0 for time, 1, 2, 3 for spatial dimensions). The term \(\partial_\mu\) represents the partial derivative with respect to the spacetime coordinate \(x^\mu\). The Lagrangian density, \(\mathcal{L}\), is a function that encapsulates the dynamics of the field and its interactions. The term \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial (\partial_\mu \phi)}\), often referred to as the conjugate momentum density or canonical momentum, describes how the Lagrangian density changes with respect to the spacetime derivative of the field. The left side of the equation, \(\partial_\mu \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial (\partial_\mu \phi)} \right)\), represents the divergence of this conjugate momentum density. The right side, \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \phi}\), represents how the Lagrangian density changes with respect to the field itself. Thus, the Euler-Lagrange equation equates the divergence of the field's momentum density to the 'force' acting on the field, derived from the Lagrangian.
local-pdes-29dd35b3.symmetry_origin: This equation is derived from Hamilton's principle (the principle of stationary action) which states that the integral of the Lagrangian over a path or field configuration is stationary (usually a minimum) for the actual physical evolution. For a field theory, the action is given by \(S = \int d^4x \mathcal{L}\). Applying the calculus of variations to this action, requiring \(\delta S = 0\) for arbitrary variations \(\delta \phi\) of the field (that vanish at the boundaries of spacetime), leads directly to the Euler-Lagrange equation.
local-pdes-29dd35b3.limits_and_boundary: The equation is a differential equation that holds locally throughout spacetime. Its implications are determined by the specific form of the Lagrangian \(\mathcal{L}\) and the boundary conditions imposed on the field \(\phi\) and its derivatives at the limits of the domain of spacetime considered. In asymptotic regions where the field \(\phi\) and its derivatives might vanish or become constant, the equation simplifies, potentially revealing conserved quantities or specific asymptotic behaviors of the field. For example, if \(\phi\) and \(\partial_\mu \phi\) are constant everywhere, the equation reduces to \(0 = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \phi}\), which implies that any constant field configuration must be at a stationary point of the Lagrangian with respect to \(\phi\).
local-pdes-29dd35b3.conceptual_definition: The provided equation, \(\partial_\mu \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial (\partial_\mu \phi)} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \phi}\), represents the Euler-Lagrange equation for a system described by a Lagrangian \(\mathcal{L}\) in the context of classical field theory. It is a fundamental equation of motion that dictates how a field, denoted by \(\phi\), evolves over spacetime. This equation arises from the principle of least action, stating that the physical path taken by a system is the one for which the action (the integral of the Lagrangian over time) is minimized. The Euler-Lagrange equation provides a more general formulation that can be applied to fields, which are functions of spacetime coordinates, rather than just point particles.
local-pdes-29dd35b3.intuitive_summary: This equation states that the rate of change of the 'momentum' conjugate to a field's gradient must equal the rate of change of the field itself within the Lagrangian density.

the-logic-check-4c3c2744.title: The Logic Check

M_{EW}.name: Electroweak Energy Scale
M_{EW}.description: The characteristic energy scale of the electroweak interaction, where the electromagnetic and weak nuclear forces unify. In particle physics, this is often related to the masses of the W and Z bosons, approximately 100 GeV.

\\(M\\).name: Total Mass / Magnetization
\\(M\\).description: The total inertial mass of a system, or net magnetic dipole moment density.

the-logic-check-4c3c2744.interpretation:
In the equation 
$M_{EW} / M_{Pl} 	sim 10^{-17}$
, 
$M_{EW}$
 represents the characteristic energy scale associated with the electroweak interaction, which unifies the electromagnetic and weak nuclear forces. This scale is approximately 
$100 	\text{GeV}$

photon-difference-0bc21506.interpretation: The equation   * = -g_{} + \frac{k_ k_}{M^2} represents a polarization sum for a vector boson, such as a photon. The left-hand side,  *, denotes the sum over all possible polarization vectors _, where _* is its complex conjugate.  In the context of a massless vector boson (like a photon), this sum should reproduce the structure of its propagator.  The right-hand side provides this structure.  The term -g_{} is related to the transverse polarizations (those perpendicular to the momentum).  The term \frac{k_ k_}{M^2} is related to the longitudinal polarization. In standard quantum electrodynamics (QED) for massless photons, the sum over physical polarizations (two transverse) is typically represented in a gauge-invariant manner. However, in intermediate steps of calculations, it's often convenient to work with a larger set of states that includes unphysical polarizations, and this identity helps manage those. The presence of M^2 suggests a context where a mass-like term might be introduced for regularization or in specific theoretical frameworks (e.g., Proca theory for massive vector bosons, or certain gauge choices in QED that might manifest a 'mass' in intermediate calculations, though photons are fundamentally massless).  If M is interpreted as a mass parameter, the term \frac{k_ k_}{M^2} would correspond to the longitudinal polarization, which is absent for massless photons but present for massive vector bosons.
photon-difference-0bc21506.symmetry_origin: This identity is a manifestation of gauge symmetry and completeness relations in quantum field theory. For massless vector bosons like photons, gauge invariance dictates that only two transverse polarization states are physical. However, in intermediate calculations, particularly when dealing with propagators in covariant gauges, it's common to sum over a larger set of states, including unphysical longitudinal and scalar polarizations, which are then carefully handled by gauge-fixing terms or are shown to cancel out in physical observables. This specific form of the completeness relation, especially with the k_ k_/M^2 term, can arise in the context of covariant quantization schemes where a gauge parameter is involved, or in extensions to massive vector bosons (Proca theory). The left side is a sum over a basis, and the right side is its representation in a specific covariant formalism.
photon-difference-0bc21506.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where the momentum k_ approaches zero (i.e., a static or zero-energy photon), the second term on the right-hand side, \frac{k_ k_}{M^2}, also goes to zero. This leaves   *  — -g_{}, which is characteristic of the polarization sum for a massless vector particle in the limit of zero momentum. If M were to approach infinity, the second term \frac{k_ k_}{M^2} would also tend to zero, again leaving -g_{}. This suggests that for very large M (or in the massless limit if M is related to a mass parameter), the contribution from the longitudinal polarization becomes negligible, consistent with the physics of massless photons having only transverse polarizations.
photon-difference-0bc21506.conceptual_definition: This formula is a completeness relation, specifically a polarization identity, that arises in the context of quantum field theory, particularly in the description of vector bosons like photons. It expresses the fact that any vector field can be decomposed into a sum over a complete basis of polarization states.  The left-hand side represents a sum over all possible polarization states, and the right-hand side provides an explicit form for this sum in terms of the metric tensor and the momentum of the particle, effectively ensuring that the full set of states correctly reproduces the propagator of a massless vector boson.
photon-difference-0bc21506.intuitive_summary: This equation is a statement of completeness for photon polarization states, ensuring that the sum over all possible ways a photon can be polarized correctly reflects its propagation properties.

observation-6e42aa5a.interpretation:

strong-form-condition-f5e20a06.title: Strong Form Condition

\\mathbf{\\tau}_{int}.name: Net Internal Torque
\\mathbf{\\tau}_{int}.description: The vector sum of all torques exerted by particles within a system on each other. It is a measure of the net rotational effect of internal forces within the system.

\\mathbf{r}_1 - \\mathbf{r}_2.name: Relative Position Vector
\\mathbf{r}_1 - \\mathbf{r}_2.description: The vector pointing from the position of particle 2 (\mathbf{r}_2) to the position of particle 1 (\mathbf{r}_1). It defines the lever arm for the force acting between the two particles.

\\mathbf{F}_{21}.name: Force Exerted by Particle 2 on Particle 1
\\mathbf{F}_{21}.description: The force vector that particle 2 applies to particle 1. According to Newton's third law, this force is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force particle 1 exerts on particle 2 (\mathbf{\mathbf{F}_{12}}).

\\(\\tau\\).name: Infinitesimal Volume Element
\\(\\tau\\).description: An infinitesimal region of space over which a volume integration is performed.

\\(r\\).name: Radial Distance / Radius

\\(F\\).description: The magnitude of an interaction that causes an object with mass to accelerate.

strong-form-condition-f5e20a06.interpretation: The equation \mathbf{\tau}\text{_int} = (\mathbf{\mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{\mathbf{r}_2}) \times \mathbf{\mathbf{F}_{21}} = 0 describes the net internal torque \mathbf{\tau}\text{_int} on a system of particles. \mathbf{\mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{\mathbf{r}_2} represents the relative position vector from particle 2 to particle 1. \mathbf{\mathbf{F}_{21}} is the force exerted by particle 2 on particle 1. The cross product signifies the torque, which is a measure of the rotational effect of a force. The condition = 0 implies that for the net internal torque to be zero, either the relative position vector is parallel to the force (which is not physically possible for a force causing acceleration, as per Newton's third law), or the force vector is zero (no interaction), or, most importantly, the sum of these torques over all pairs of interacting particles in the system cancels out. This cancellation arises from Newton's third law, where \mathbf{\mathbf{F}_{21}} = -\mathbf{\mathbf{F}_{12}}, and the torques due to action-reaction pairs sum to zero: (\mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2) \times \mathbf{\mathbf{F}_{21}} + (\mathbf{r}_2 - \mathbf{r}_1) \times \mathbf{\mathbf{F}_{12}} = (\mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2) \times (\mathbf{\mathbf{F}_{21}} - (\mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2) \times \mathbf{\mathbf{F}_{21}} = 0.
strong-form-condition-f5e20a06.symmetry_origin: This condition is a direct consequence of Newton's third law of motion (action-reaction principle) and the definition of torque. For any two particles in an isolated system, the force exerted by particle 1 on particle 2 (\mathbf{\mathbf{F}_{12}}) is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force exerted by particle 2 on particle 1 (\mathbf{\mathbf{F}_{21}}). The total internal torque is the sum of the torques from all such pairs. Since the forces are equal and opposite, and they act along the line connecting the particles (for central forces, which is a common scenario where this is particularly clear), the torques produced by these action-reaction pairs cancel each other out, leading to a zero net internal torque. This is equivalent to the conservation of angular momentum for the system.
strong-form-condition-f5e20a06.limits_and_boundary: If the relative position vector \mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2} approaches zero, it implies that the two particles are at the same location, which is not physically possible for distinct particles. In such a limit, the concept of separate forces and torques breaks down. If the force \mathbf{\mathbf{F}_{21}} approaches zero (i.e., no interaction between particles), then the torque is trivially zero. If the force is finite but the particles are infinitely far apart (|\mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2|| \to \infty), and the force magnitude diminishes with distance (e.g., inverse square law), the torque may still be zero if the force effectively becomes negligible at infinite separation. The condition \mathbf{\tau}\text{_int} = 0 is fundamentally about isolated systems; if external torques are present, this condition will not hold, and the system's angular momentum will change.
strong-form-condition-f5e20a06.conceptual_definition:
The strong form condition for the conservation of angular momentum, in the context of classical mechanics, states that the net internal torque acting on a system of particles is zero if the system is isolated in terms of its interactions.
This condition implies that the total angular momentum of the system remains constant over time. The internal torque is defined as the cross product of the relative position vector between two interacting particles and the force exerted by one particle on the other. For a system composed of multiple particles, the sum of these torques over all pairs of interacting particles must be zero for the net internal torque to be zero.
strong-form-condition-f5e20a06.intuitive_summary: For an isolated system, the internal forces between its parts exert no net twisting effect (torque) on the system as a whole, thus preserving its total rotational motion (angular momentum).

london-penetration-depth-aeb428eb.interpretation: The formula λ_L = √(m / (μ_0 n_s e^2)) reveals the physical origins of magnetic field penetration in superconductors. The mass of the charge carriers, denoted by m, appears in the numerator, indicating that heavier charge carriers will lead to a larger penetration depth. The term μ_0, the permeability of free space, is a fundamental constant related to magnetic fields. The density of superconducting charge carriers, n_s, is in the denominator, meaning a higher density of these carriers results in a shorter penetration depth, as they can more effectively screen the magnetic field. The elementary charge, e, also in the denominator, reflects the fact that these charge carriers are fundamental particles. Squaring e signifies that the strength of the screening depends on the magnitude of the charge. Thus, a superconductor with light, highly mobile charge carriers and a high density of these carriers will exhibit a small London penetration depth, meaning magnetic fields are expelled very effectively.
london-penetration-depth-aeb428eb.symmetry_origin: The London penetration depth arises from the electrodynamics of superconductors, specifically the London equations, which describe the motion of superconducting charge carriers (Cooper pairs) under the influence of electromagnetic fields. These equations are derived from considering the response of a charged superfluid to electromagnetic forces, leading to a relationship between the current density and the magnetic field that exhibits a characteristic length scale, the penetration depth. This length scale emerges from the inertia of the charge carriers and their density, reflecting the underlying quantum mechanical nature of superconductivity.
london-penetration-depth-aeb428eb.limits_and_boundary: As the density of superconducting charge carriers n_s approaches zero (a non-superconducting state), the London penetration depth λ_L approaches infinity, indicating that magnetic fields penetrate completely. Conversely, as n_s increases, λ_L decreases, implying stronger expulsion of magnetic fields. If the mass of the charge carriers m were to approach zero, λ_L would also approach zero, signifying perfect diamagnetism where magnetic fields are instantaneously and completely excluded. However, this limit is not physically attainable due to the finite mass of the charge carriers involved in superconductivity.
london-penetration-depth-aeb428eb.conceptual_definition: The London penetration depth, denoted by λ_L, quantifies the characteristic distance over which an external magnetic field penetrates into a superconductor in the absence of an applied magnetic field. In the Meissner effect, an ideal superconductor expels magnetic fields from its interior. However, for any real superconductor, there is a finite depth to which the magnetic field can penetrate before being completely screened by surface currents.
london-penetration-depth-aeb428eb.intuitive_summary: The London penetration depth is the distance a magnetic field decays to 1/e of its surface value inside a superconductor.

ckm-unitary-triangle-closure-relation-91.title: CKM Unitary Triangle
ckm-unitary-triangle-closure-relation-91.interpretation:
The equation represents a fundamental constraint derived from the unitarity of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix, denoted by 

$$V = \begin{pmatrix} V_{ud} & V_{us} & V_{ub} \\ V_{cd} & V_{cs} & V_{cb} \\ V_{td} & V_{ts} & V_{tb} \end{pmatrix}$$ 

This matrix describes the coupling of quarks to the W boson in weak interactions, and its unitarity means that its rows and columns are orthonormal vectors. The equation specifically arises from the orthogonality of the first and third columns of the CKM matrix: the dot product of the first column 

$$(V_{ud}, V_{cd}, V_{td})$$ 

and the complex conjugate of the third column 

$$(V_{ub}^*, V_{cb}^*, V_{tb}^*)$$

is zero. Each term 

$$V_{ij}V_{kl}^*$$ 

represents a product of two CKM matrix elements, which are complex numbers that quantify the strength and phase of the weak interaction transitions between different quark flavors. The phases in these complex numbers are the source of CP violation. The fact that their sum is zero geometrically implies that these three complex numbers can be represented as three vectors in the complex plane that add up to zero, forming a closed triangle. The shape and area of this triangle are crucial for testing the consistency of the Standard Model and precisely measuring the parameters related to CP violation.
ckm-unitary-triangle-closure-relation-91.symmetry_origin:
The origin of this equation lies in the unitarity property of the CKM matrix, which is a consequence of the conservation of probability in quantum mechanics and the structure of the electroweak interaction. Specifically, the CKM matrix is a unitary matrix, meaning that its transpose conjugate is its inverse, 

$$V^\nabla V = I$$ 

where 

$$V^\nabla$$ 

is the conjugate transpose of 

$$V$$ 

and 

$$I$$ 

is the identity matrix. The equation 

$$V_{ud}V_{ub}^* + V_{cd}V_{cb}^* + V_{td}V_{tb}^* = 0$$ 
is derived from the condition that the dot product of the first column vector 

$$(V_{ud}, V_{cd}, V_{td})^T$$ 

and the complex conjugate of the third column vector 

$$(V_{ub}^*, V_{cb}^*, V_{tb}^*)^T$$ 
is zero, i.e., 

$$ \begin{pmatrix} V_{ud} & V_{cd} & V_{td} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} V_{ub}^* \\ V_{cb}^* \\ V_{tb}^* \end{pmatrix} = 0 $$ 
This condition is a direct manifestation of the orthogonality of the column vectors of a unitary matrix.
ckm-unitary-triangle-closure-relation-91.limits_and_boundary:
This equation is an identity that holds true for any set of parameters that satisfy the unitarity of the CKM matrix. It does not have asymptotic limits in the sense of variables approaching zero or infinity, as the CKM matrix elements are themselves parameters determined by experimental measurements. However, if one were to hypothetically consider scenarios where certain CKM matrix elements were zero (e.g., if there were no mixing between certain generations), the structure of the triangle would be significantly altered or collapse. For instance, if all terms involving the third generation quarks were absent (i.e., 

$$V_{ub} = V_{cb} = V_{td} = V_{tb} = 0$$), then the equation would trivially become 

$$0 + 0 + 0 = 0$$ 
which would not provide any information about CP violation. The non-zero nature of these terms and their complex phases are what give the CKM Unitary Triangle its meaningful shape and its significance in probing CP violation.

ckm-unitary-triangle-closure-relation-91.conceptual_definition:
The CKM Unitary Triangle is a graphical representation of a fundamental relationship within the Standard Model of particle physics that encodes information about the mixing of quarks. The equation 
$$V_{ud}V_{ub}^* + V_{cd}V_{cb}^* + V_{td}V_{tb}^* = 0$$ 
states that the sum of three complex numbers, formed by products of elements of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix, is zero. When represented as vectors in the complex plane, these three products form a triangle, hence the name 'Unitary Triangle'. The vertices of this triangle correspond to specific combinations of quark couplings, and its shape (specifically, its area and the angles within it) is sensitive to CP violation in the weak interactions.
ckm-unitary-triangle-closure-relation-91.intuitive_summary: The unitarity of the CKM matrix implies that the sum of three specific products of its elements is zero, forming a triangle in the complex plane that reveals the extent of CP violation.

kolmogorov-energy-spectrum-power-law-db8.title: Kolmogorov Energy Spectrum
kolmogorov-energy-spectrum-power-law-db8.interpretation: The Kolmogorov energy spectrum equation quantifies the distribution of kinetic energy within a turbulent fluid. The term \( E(k) \) represents the energy spectral density, which is the energy per unit wavenumber (or per unit logarithmic interval of wavenumber). Wavenumber \( k \) is inversely related to spatial length scale \( L \) by \( k = 2π/L \), so a higher \( k \) corresponds to smaller eddies and finer scales. The term \( \epsilon \) (epsilon) is the mean rate of energy dissipation per unit mass into thermal energy, often referred to as the energy dissipation rate. This quantity represents the overall intensity of the turbulence. \( C \) is a dimensionless universal constant, known as the Kolmogorov constant, whose value is approximately 1.4 to 2.0. The equation \( E(k) = C \epsilon^{2/3} k^{-5/3} \) shows that as wavenumber \( k \) increases (meaning we look at smaller eddies), the energy spectral density \( E(k) \) decreases, following a power law with an exponent of -5/3. This implies that smaller eddies contain less energy than larger eddies, but the energy is distributed across a wide range of scales.
kolmogorov-energy-spectrum-power-law-db8.symmetry_origin: The Kolmogorov energy spectrum arises from dimensional analysis and statistical considerations of homogeneous and isotropic turbulence. It relies on the concept of energy cascading from large scales (where energy is injected) to small scales (where it is dissipated by viscosity). The derivation assumes that in the inertial subrange, the statistics of the turbulent eddies are determined only by the energy dissipation rate \( \epsilon \) and the wavenumber \( k \). This invariance to the specific details of the large-scale forcing or small-scale dissipation mechanisms, as long as they are separated in scale, is a key aspect of its universality.
kolmogorov-energy-spectrum-power-law-db8.limits_and_boundary: The Kolmogorov energy spectrum is valid for the inertial subrange of turbulence, which lies between the integral scale (where energy is injected) and the dissipation scale (where viscous effects become dominant). At very small wavenumbers (large scales), the energy spectrum is typically dominated by the energy injection mechanism and does not follow the \( k^{-5/3} \) power law. At very large wavenumbers (small scales), viscous dissipation becomes important, and the spectrum drops off much more rapidly than \( k^{-5/3} \), often described by a different power law or an exponential decay. The \( k^{-5/3} \) spectrum is characteristic of the intermediate scales where energy is neither created nor dissipated but simply transferred across scales.

E(k).name: Energy Spectrum
E(k).description: The energy spectral density, representing the kinetic energy per unit wavenumber in a turbulent flow. Its units are the square of velocity, which is energy per unit mass.

C.name: Kolmogorov Constant
C.description: A dimensionless universal constant that appears in the Kolmogorov theory of turbulence.

\\epsilon.name: Energy Dissipation Rate
\\epsilon.description: The mean rate of kinetic energy dissipation per unit mass into thermal energy in a turbulent flow.

k.name: Wavenumber
k.description: A measure of the spatial frequency of turbulent eddies, inversely related to the characteristic length scale of the eddies (i.e., k = 2π/L).

\\(E\\).name: Electric Field Strength
\\(E\\).description: The magnitude of the electric field vector, representing the force per unit charge at a point in space.

kolmogorov-energy-spectrum-power-law-db8.conceptual_definition: The Kolmogorov energy spectrum, denoted by the equation \( E(k) = C \epsilon^{2/3} k^{-5/3} \), is a fundamental result in the statistical theory of turbulence. It describes how energy is distributed across different spatial scales (or equivalently, wavenumbers) in a turbulent flow. Specifically, it predicts that in the inertial subrange of turbulence, where energy is neither created by large-scale instabilities nor dissipated by viscosity, the energy per unit wavenumber \( E(k) \) is proportional to the rate of energy dissipation \( \epsilon \) raised to the power of 2/3 and inversely proportional to the wavenumber \( k \) raised to the power of 5/3.
kolmogorov-energy-spectrum-power-law-db8.intuitive_summary: In turbulent flows, energy cascades from large scales to small scales, with the energy content at each scale being determined by the rate at which energy is injected and dissipated.

longitudinal-polarization-identity-1-434.title: Longitudinal Polarization Vector of Massive Vector Bosons
longitudinal-polarization-identity-1-434.interpretation: \( m \) is the boson mass, \( \mathbf{k} \) is the spatial momentum vector, and \( \omega \) is the energy/frequency.
longitudinal-polarization-identity-1-434.symmetry_origin: Poincaré covariance and Higgs mechanism in electroweak gauge theory.
longitudinal-polarization-identity-1-434.limits_and_boundary: In the high-energy limit \( \omega \gg m \), the polarization vector behaves as \( \epsilon_L^\mu \approx k^\mu / m \), which leads to Goldstone boson equivalence.

longitudinal-polarization-identity-1-434.intuitive_summary: Massive spin-1 particles possess a third polarization state pointing along their direction of motion, whose amplitude scales inversely with their mass at high energies.

logical-basis-ontology-identity-1-ce0a3e.title: Quantum Logic Lattice Non-Distributivity Relation
logical-basis-ontology-identity-1-ce0a3e.interpretation: \( P, Q, R \) are propositions (represented as projection operators on a Hilbert space), \( \land \) is the meet (logical AND), and \( \lor \) is the join (logical OR).
logical-basis-ontology-identity-1-ce0a3e.symmetry_origin: Non-commutativity of projection operators in quantum mechanics.
logical-basis-ontology-identity-1-ce0a3e.limits_and_boundary: If all projection operators commute, the distributivity equality holds, recovering classical Boolean logic.
logical-basis-ontology-identity-1-ce0a3e.conceptual_definition: In quantum logic (developed by Birkhoff and von Neumann), propositions form an orthomodular lattice where the distributive law of classical logic fails, replaced by this weaker modular/orthomodular inequality.
logical-basis-ontology-identity-1-ce0a3e.intuitive_summary: In the quantum world, saying 'P is true AND (either Q or R is true)' does not mean the same thing as 'either (P and Q) or (P and R) is true', because measuring one property changes the system's state.

navier-stokes-momentum-fluids-27e5bf4d.title: Navier-Stokes Momentum Equation (Fluid Dynamics and Nonlinear Systems)
navier-stokes-momentum-fluids-27e5bf4d.symmetry_origin: The Navier-Stokes equations are derived from the fundamental principles of conservation of momentum, which is a consequence of the translational symmetry of physical laws (as stated by Noether's theorem). They can also be derived by applying Newton's second law to an infinitesimal fluid parcel and considering all relevant forces: pressure forces, viscous stresses, and external body forces. The equations are generally coordinate-invariant, meaning they hold true regardless of the chosen coordinate system.
navier-stokes-momentum-fluids-27e5bf4d.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of zero viscosity (\boldsymbol{\boldsymbol{\nabla}} \to 0), the Navier-Stokes equations reduce to the Euler equations, which describe the motion of ideal, inviscid fluids. In this limit, viscous dissipation is absent, and phenomena like boundary layers do not exist. Conversely, for very low Reynolds numbers (Re \to 0), which typically occur for highly viscous fluids or very slow flows, the inertial terms (\rho \frac{\text{D}\textbf{u}}{\text{D}t}) become negligible compared to the viscous terms, leading to Stokes flow (creeping flow), where the flow is dominated by viscous forces and is often reversible. The equations are also subject to boundary conditions, such as no-slip conditions at solid surfaces (where fluid velocity matches the surface velocity) or free-surface conditions.

navier-stokes-momentum-fluids-27e5bf4d.conceptual_definition: The Navier-Stokes momentum equation is a fundamental partial differential equation in fluid dynamics that describes the motion of viscous fluid substances. It is a statement of Newton's second law of motion, \textit{F} = m\textit{a}, applied to fluid elements. The equation balances the forces acting on a fluid element with its mass times acceleration, considering inertial forces, pressure gradients, viscous forces, and external body forces.
navier-stokes-momentum-fluids-27e5bf4d.intuitive_summary: This equation states that the rate of change of momentum of a fluid element is equal to the sum of forces acting upon it: pressure forces, viscous forces, and external body forces.
